title: Blob storage and uploads
tagline: Keep bytes in object storage, metadata in a database, and never stream big files through your API servers.
why:
Files (attachments, photos, CSVs, video) are large, written once and read many times. A database is the wrong home: a 20 MB row bloats backups, replication and every query that touches the table. Object storage such as S3 stores the bytes cheaply, durably and with no capacity planning, and your database keeps a small row that says who owns the file, where it is and what state it is in.

The second idea is to keep bytes off your app servers. If a 100 MB upload streams through your API, it ties up a worker for a minute and your fleet scales on bandwidth instead of requests. A presigned URL lets the browser send the bytes straight to the bucket, with your API only handing out short-lived permission.

Uploaded files are untrusted input. Scanning, resizing and parsing happen asynchronously after the upload, and the file is not usable until they finish.
how:
1. Ask for permission. The client calls POST /uploads {name, type, size}. The API checks auth, type and size, writes a metadata row with status = pending, and returns a presigned URL for a server-chosen key like quarantine/7f3c.... The URL is valid for a few minutes and only for that key.

2. Upload directly. The browser PUTs the bytes to the bucket. Large files use multipart upload: parts of 5 MB to 5 GB (only the last part may be smaller), sent in parallel, retried one part at a time. A presigned POST policy can enforce a size range; a presigned PUT can at most pin an exact Content-Length.

3. React to the upload. The bucket emits an ObjectCreated event to a queue. Delivery is at least once, so every handler must be idempotent (key on the object key and its ETag). Scope the event to the quarantine/ prefix, or moving a clean file fires another event.

4. Process asynchronously. A scanner (for example ClamAV, or a managed malware scanner) checks the file. Clean files move to the clean prefix and the row becomes clean; infected ones are deleted and the row becomes rejected. Only then do other workers make thumbnails, parse the CSV or extract text.

5. Serve it. Downloads use short-lived presigned GET URLs, often through a CDN, with Content-Disposition: attachment so an uploaded HTML or SVG file cannot run as a page on your domain.

Lifecycle. Rules move old objects to cheaper storage classes and delete abandoned pending uploads and incomplete multipart parts after a day or two.

steps.note: The client asks to upload report.pdf, 40 MB. The API checks the user may upload, the type is allowed and the size is under the limit.
Insert a row: owner, server-chosen object key, size, status = pending. The key is generated by the server, never taken from the file name.
Return a presigned URL valid for about 5 minutes, for that one key only. No cloud credentials ever reach the browser.
The browser uploads straight to the bucket. Files over ~100 MB use multipart upload so a dropped connection retries one part, not the whole file.
The object sits in a quarantine/ prefix that nothing serves from. Storage writes it across several devices and zones before acknowledging.
The bucket emits ObjectCreated to a queue. Events are at least once and can arrive twice, so handlers must be idempotent.
A scanner worker streams the object and checks it. It scales on queue depth, so a burst of uploads becomes backlog, not failures.
Clean: move the object to the clean prefix and set status = clean. Infected: delete it and set rejected, and tell the user.
Only clean files go on to further processing. Here a resize job is queued for images.
Write three sizes under derived keys. Generating thumbnails eagerly costs storage; doing it on first request costs latency. Eager is simpler for a few fixed sizes.
The client polls the file's status or gets a push. Until it says clean, the file cannot be downloaded or attached.

tradeoffs.pro: App servers never touch the bytes; uploads scale with the storage service, not your fleet.
tradeoffs.con: Validation moves after the upload: you need events, a quarantine prefix and cleanup of abandoned uploads.

tradeoffs.pro: Simple; you can validate and scan in the request.
tradeoffs.con: Large files hold workers and memory for minutes; request timeouts and load balancer limits bite.

tradeoffs.pro: One store, transactional with the metadata.
tradeoffs.con: Bloats backups and replicas, costs more per GB, and slows the database. Fine only for small files in small numbers.

tradeoffs.pro: Eager thumbnails are ready when needed; on-demand (resize at first request, then cache) stores only what is used.
tradeoffs.con: Eager wastes work on files nobody views; on-demand adds latency to the first view and needs a cache.

numbers: S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability, by storing data across several devices in at least 3 availability zones.
One S3 PUT can be up to 5 GB. Larger objects need multipart upload: parts of 5 MB to 5 GB, at most 10,000 parts.
Request rate per prefix: about 3,500 writes/s and 5,500 reads/s. Spread hot workloads over several prefixes.
Presigned URLs signed with SigV4 can last at most 7 days; in practice use 5 to 15 minutes.
Sizing: 1M uploads/day × 2 MB average = 2 TB/day, about 730 TB a year before lifecycle rules.
Since December 2020, S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs and DELETEs.
say: The client asks my API for a presigned URL, uploads directly to S3, and my API only stores a metadata row, so big files never pass through the app servers.
Uploads land in a quarantine prefix; an ObjectCreated event triggers a virus scan, and only clean files are moved, processed and made downloadable.
Event handlers are idempotent because storage events are delivered at least once, and lifecycle rules clean up abandoned uploads.
pitfalls: Using the user's file name as the object key. It leaks data, collides, and invites path tricks. Generate the key on the server.
Serving uploads inline from your main domain. An uploaded HTML or SVG file then runs script as your site. Use a separate domain and Content-Disposition: attachment.

Assuming a presigned PUT enforces a size limit. Unless you sign an exact Content-Length, it does not; use a presigned POST with a content-length range, or check the size when the event arrives and delete oversized files.
Making files available before the scan finishes. The status must gate every download path.
Forgetting cleanup: abandoned pending rows and incomplete multipart uploads keep costing money until a lifecycle rule removes them.

quiz.q: Why give the client a presigned URL instead of accepting the upload on your API?
options: The bytes go straight to object storage, so app servers are not tied up by large uploads
It removes the need for authentication
quiz.why: The API only authorises and records metadata. Bandwidth and retries are the storage service's problem, and your fleet scales on requests, not bytes.

quiz.q: Your thumbnail worker sometimes produces the same thumbnail twice. What is the most likely reason?
options: Storage event notifications are at least once, so the handler ran twice
quiz.why: Object events can be delivered more than once. Make the handler idempotent, for example by writing to a deterministic key derived from the source key.

quiz.q: Where should a newly uploaded file live until the virus scan passes?
options: In a quarantine prefix that nothing serves from
Directly in the public CDN path
In the database as a blob
quiz.why: Untrusted files are isolated until scanned. Only clean files are moved to where downloads and other processors can see them.
